name: AD8495ARMZ-R7
title: AD8494/AD8495/AD8496/AD8497: thermocouple amplifiers with built-in cold junction compensation, 5 mV/°C output, MSOP-8
summary: A fixed-gain instrumentation amplifier and an on-chip temperature sensor that turn a thermocouple voltage directly into 5 mV/°C. The AD8494 (gain 96.7) and AD8496 (gain 90.35) are trimmed for J type thermocouples, the AD8495 and AD8497 (gain 122.4) for K type; the AD8494/AD8495 are tuned for a 0°C to 50°C ambient and the AD8496/AD8497 for 25°C to 100°C. Each comes in an A grade and a tighter C grade (1°C initial accuracy). It runs from 2.7 V to 36 V single or ±2.7 V to ±18 V, draws 180 µA, withstands inputs 25 V past the opposite rail, and can also serve as a Celsius thermometer or a setpoint controller.

tables.title: Electrical characteristics
tables.conditions: +VS = 5 V, −VS = 0 V, V+IN = V−IN = 0 V, VREF = 0 V, TA = TRJ = 25°C, RL = 100 kΩ, unless otherwise noted. Figures exclude the thermocouple's own gain and offset errors. TA: ambient temperature at the AD849x; TRJ: thermocouple reference junction temperature; TMJ: thermocouple measurement junction temperature.
notes: (1) The figure is the shift in the reading, in °C, per °C change of the cold junction: the slope of the straight line between the errors at 0°C and 50°C ambient (AD8494, AD8495) or at 25°C and 100°C ambient (AD8496, AD8497).
(2) Thermocouple gain error and thermocouple nonlinearity are excluded.

(3) With RL = 100 kΩ, measurement junctions above about 880°C (AD8494, AD8496) or 960°C (AD8495, AD8497) need a supply above 5 V or a negative REF voltage; measurement junctions below 5°C need a positive REF offset or a negative supply.
(4) The inputs are PNP transistors: bias current always leaves the part.
(5) A large output current warms the die and raises the CJC error.
(6) Unequal supplies may be used, provided the thermocouple common-mode voltage stays inside the input voltage range.

circuits.title: Negative input grounded through 1 MΩ for open thermocouple detection
circuits.description: The thermocouple joins the two inputs; a 1 MΩ resistor takes the inverting lead to ground. If the thermocouple opens, the bias current flowing out of +IN has no return and drives that input up, so the output goes to the positive rail.

circuits.title: Input filter for any thermocouple style
circuits.description: A series resistor R in each lead with a capacitor CD across the two inputs and a capacitor CC from each input to ground forms a low-pass filter that keeps RF off the inputs. CD sets the differential corner and CC the common-mode corner; CD is at least ten times CC. R stays under 50 kΩ so the offset current makes no measurable error. The 1 MΩ to ground on the inverting lead, ahead of R, is fitted when the thermocouple tip type is not known.

parts.note: fitted when the tip type is unknown

circuits.title: Thermocouple grounded through a 1 MΩ resistor
circuits.description: One resistor from the inverting input to ground on the board gives the thermocouple its only ground reference. With an insulated tip it is low enough that no common-mode voltage builds up; with a grounded or exposed tip it is high enough that little current flows from the tip to ground. 100 kΩ to 1 MΩ is the range.

circuits.title: Driving the reference pin
circuits.description: A divider from a voltage V sets the REF level, and an AD8613 wired as a voltage follower drives the REF pin from it, so REF sees a low source impedance. Driving REF straight from the divider is the wrong way; the OP777 also suits the buffer.

circuits.title: Basic connection
circuits.description: A J or K type thermocouple reaches +IN and −IN through an RC input filter, with 1 MΩ from the inverting lead to ground for open thermocouple detection and a ground reference. SENSE ties to OUT and REF to ground, so OUT = TMJ × 5 mV/°C. The part runs from 5 V with −VS at ground; +VS has 0.1 µF at the pin and a 10 µF tantalum that may sit further away and be shared. The second 0.1 µF and 10 µF pair decouples −VS when a negative supply is used.
notes: C6 and C7 sit on −VS, which is grounded with a single supply.

circuits.title: Ambient temperature sensor
circuits.description: Both inputs are shorted to ground, so the thermocouple path reads zero and the output carries only the internal cold junction sensor: a Celsius thermometer giving VOUT = TA × 5 mV/°C. SENSE ties to OUT, REF and −VS to ground, +VS to 5 V. The AD8494 suits this use best; the other three work but their slope is not exactly 5 mV/°C (AN-1087 gives the exact transfer functions).

circuits.title: Setpoint controller
circuits.description: SENSE is taken off OUT and driven by a setpoint voltage instead: OUT swings to −VS while the measured temperature is under the setpoint and to +VS once it is over. The thermocouple input has the usual RC filter and 1 MΩ to ground. A low-impedance setpoint source keeps accuracy and CMRR; a divider needs a buffer.

circuits.title: Setpoint controller with 10 degrees of hysteresis
circuits.description: The setpoint controller with a divider from OUT to ground whose midpoint drives REF: R2 = 100 kΩ from OUT and R1 = 1 kΩ to ground feed back about 1 % of the output swing, giving THYST = VS × R1/(R1 + R2)/(5 mV/°C), about 10°C at 5 V. A 1 kΩ in series with SENSE matches the divider's source resistance to keep CMRR.

operation.text: A thermocouple gives a voltage set by the temperature difference between its measurement (hot) junction and its reference (cold) junction, where its wires meet the copper of the board. The signal is tens of microvolts per °C. To read the hot junction alone, the cold junction temperature must be measured and its contribution cancelled; the AD849x does this with an internal temperature sensor, so the J type example gives 250 mV for a 50°C hot junction whether the cold junction is at 0°C or 50°C.

A low-offset instrumentation amplifier of fixed gain sums with the cold junction sensor to make 5 mV/°C. The gain differs per part to keep 5 mV/°C over its thermocouple's range: 96.7 for the AD8494, 90.35 for the AD8496 (both J type) and 122.4 for the AD8495 and AD8497 (K type). High common-mode rejection blocks noise picked up on long leads, and the high-impedance inputs allow added filtering.

The AD8494/AD8495 compensation is set for a laboratory ambient around 25°C and is specified from 0°C to 50°C. The AD8496/AD8497 compensation is set for a hotter ambient around 60°C and is specified from 25°C to 100°C; automotive, autoclave and oven uses are its examples.

With no load the part draws 180 µA typical, which keeps self-heating low, and it can drive more than ±5 mA. On a single 5 V supply the 5 mV/°C output spans close to 1000 degrees. It works from supplies under 3 V for direct connection to low-voltage ADCs and up to 36 V where a wide common-mode range is needed.

The input transistors are PNP, so bias current flows out of both inputs. An input left floating is pulled high and the output saturates. With −IN returned to ground through 1 MΩ, a broken thermocouple drives the output to the positive rail.

Each input tolerates up to 25 V beyond the opposite supply rail: with +5 V and −3 V supplies the inputs may sit anywhere from −20 V to +22 V. REF and SENSE must stay within 0.3 V of the supply rails. The inputs withstand 4 kV ESD.

The maximum error is built from five parts: initial calibration accuracy (removable with a one-point calibration), ambient temperature rejection (at 0.025°C/°C a 20°C shift of the cold junction adds under 0.5°C), gain error away from the calibration point (removable with a two-point calibration, usually negligible), the thermocouple's own manufacturing tolerance, and thermocouple nonlinearity, which stays under ±2°C within the ranges of the accuracy table.

A low-pass filter ahead of the inputs is strongly advised in noisy surroundings, because long thermocouple leads act as antennas; RF reaching the inputs can be rectified and show up as temperature fluctuations. Set the corner low while still passing the thermocouple signal. Keep each filter resistor below 50 kΩ so input offset current does not affect accuracy.

Return the thermocouple to ground with a 100 kΩ to 1 MΩ resistor from the inverting input on the board; this suits insulated, grounded and exposed tips alike. The inputs want exactly one ground or common-mode source: a second ground connection forms a loop through the thermocouple that can swamp its small signal.

The internal sensor measures the AD849x's own temperature, so the point where the thermocouple meets the board must sit as close to the part as possible and at the same temperature. Any difference shows up directly as error; it arises when the junction is far from the part or when the part supplies a lot of output power. Keep the traces from the junction to the part short.

REF shifts the output, which allows negative temperatures on a single supply, matches the output to a following ADC's range, and can trim out an initial calibration error by applying a small offset. Drive it from a low-impedance source such as an AD8613 or OP777 follower; a bare resistor divider on REF degrades performance.

If readings are wrong, remove the thermocouple and ground +IN and −IN. A correct ambient reading points to the thermocouple wiring, typically grounding or missing filtering; a wrong one points to the AD849x or the circuitry after it.
Put 0.1 µF right at each supply pin, on +VS and, with dual supplies, on −VS too. A 10 µF tantalum may sit further away and be shared.

With SENSE driven by a setpoint voltage instead of OUT, a temperature under the setpoint sends the output to −VS and one over it sends the output to +VS. The input can be a remote thermocouple, or the part's own sensor with the inputs grounded. Use a low-impedance setpoint source, buffering a divider. Hysteresis comes from a divider from OUT to REF, with a resistor equal to the divider's output resistance in series with SENSE to preserve CMRR.
